item.author: gmays
item.content:encoded: Introducing Pangram Image 1.0 and Pangram Image Flash 1.0A few months ago, we released Pangram Image as a research preview. We are now proud to announce Pangram Image 1.0: The state-of-the-art in both AI image and AI video detection. We would like to thank the whole community for taking the time to try it and find its weaknesses, and for holding us to a high standard to make a better detector for everyone.Our new flagship AI image detection model, , with: State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI image generatorsHeatmap output for localizing exactly where AI appears in imagesRobustness to edits, compression, and low resolutionsA smaller, faster model, with: State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI video generatorsFrame by frame analysis of AI edited videosChrome Extension support for detecting AI in your feedAPI support for image and videoWe tested our Pangram Image 1.0 model against several commercial and academic AI image detectors. We created synthetic mirrors of 100 real photos using 12 frontier state of the art AI image generators, using prompts that closely matched the original photo for a total of 1,200 synthetic images. Our model achieves 99.96% accuracy on this evaluation set.Academic AI Image Detection BenchmarksWe are committed to providing the highest quality detection to our users. To test our model robustly, we compared it against several academic benchmarks for AI image detection. Sources: X-AIGD · Mirage-Test · AIGenImages2026 · Synthbuster + RAISE comparison · Community ForensicsMany social media platforms compress and downscale images, and malicious actors can also add blur, noise, and other artifacts to try to trick AI detectors into thinking AI images are real. We specifically train to detect these kinds of transformations, and we have found our model to be robust to these edits.Our initial release limited image input to the minimum size of 512x512, as our accuracy dropped off at lower resolutions. We are now lowering this limit to 256x256, as we find our new model has improved accuracy at lower resolutions. At resolutions below 512, image detection results will come with a reduced confidence disclaimer.A recent academic study, DF26, showed that humans are barely better than random when it comes to telling real videos from AI videos of people talking. Modern detectors were not much better. This is why we are very excited to release Pangram Image Flash 1.0, a faster model that particularly excels at frontier AI video detection. On DF26 it scores 98.7%, a 29-point leap over the next best detector.To compare against the industry, we took 129 real social media videos and generated AI mirrors using 14 different frontier video generators (100 videos each, sampled from the 129 real videos). The generators were each seeded with the first real frame from the input video and then prompted with a VLM-generated description of what happens in the video to make a difficult synthetic mirror. We then compared our model against multiple major AI video detection services across the 1,529 total videos:By starting from real video frames and creating a synthetic mirror, we can evaluate the model’s ability to distinguish between two very realistic looking videos. This prevents the model from introducing bias towards calling certain types of content AI, since each real video and its mirror share the same scene and subject.Academic AI Video Detection BenchmarksWe compare our Image Flash model against several academic benchmarks for frontier AI video detection. We achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, which together include almost every frontier generation model for AI video. Sources: AIGVDBench · DF26 · Ivy-FakePangram now natively supports video upload. Upload a video and Pangram Image Flash 1.0 will analyze it frame by frame to give you a complete analysis of which parts of the video come back as AI detected.We have integrated Pangram Image 1.0 into our Chrome extension. This will flag AI-generated content while you scroll social media, online shopping, rental listings, and any other site where knowing that what you’re seeing is real matters.With the release of Pangram Image 1.0 and Flash 1.0, we updated our API to support both image and video detection. We are excited to put the capability of these models into the hands of the community.

item.title: Hungary: Communist-era files released, up to 60k former agents revealed
item.author: rdmuser
item.content:encoded: In spite of Hungary's democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum.Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar ended this stall with a bill in September to grant unrestricted access for the public to the records for the first time."After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives."For decades, restrictions on public access provided opportunities for political hysteria, blackmail, the exertion of pressure, and silencing," he said.Public figures featured in registryPoliticians, clergy members and TV personalities' names appeared in the registries. But a "large proportion" of the informants were "people who did not make their mark on national public life," said Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, the head of the archive.The government will set up hotlines offering emotional support and counselling for those affected by the revelations."Following today's disclosure, a great many families will be confronted with information that is difficult for them to bear," Magyar said, asking people to treat the disclosure with "dignity and humanity."Various types of documents disclosedUnder the law on the full disclosure of the previous regime’s secret service activities, four types of state security records dating from before 1990 will be made freely accessible to anyone.The "6 card" is the registration sheet for a network member. It contains the agent’s identifying data, including name, place and date of birth, mother’s name and occupation, but also the main details of the agent’s activity. Among them, the circumstances and motivations that led to them becoming an agent and how long they remained a network member. A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure.The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public.A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February.Around 150,000 agents during communist eraHungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent.Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment.Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime.Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes.But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office. Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total.Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete. Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent.The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them.The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation. "We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants."I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed.

item.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
item.author: NathanFlurry
item.content:encoded: Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3.Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle.It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable.When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users.As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes).For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects.Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds.Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds.It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost:When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99).We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhereRivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust. Out of the box, they support agents (Pi Durable), workflows, real-time, multiplayer, running AI-generated code, Durable Streams, and integrations with tools like Vercel’s Eve and Turso. See all of our available guides, or point your agent at them: https://rivet.dev/docs/#guidesTry it out now, by reading our quickstart guides (https://rivet.dev/docs/) or ask your agent: “Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then build a multiplayer chat agent and run it locally.”We’d love to get feedback on your experience with Rivet! We’re deeply invested in making Rivet an easy-to-self-host, flexible, and efficient way to run agentic workloads.

item.title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
item.author: pantalaimon
item.content:encoded: If you run on Alpine Linux, update now and restart . Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart . Either one closes the hole.An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a or password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024 bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without one reachable.You are affected if all of the following are true:You run the Alpine package, which is built without PAM, or you run with . ( with is not affected.) is (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it).The machine has an account whose password field is . This includes: , which ships as in the base image since about Alpine 3.16. OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so root is only reachable if is set. That does not help if another account that can log in is able to become root, for example through .Any key-only user created with without a password, or with .Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.The user in the official images (see below).At least one local account has a or password hash.Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).Docker and other container users that do not run in the container.Systems with PasswordAuthentication no.Systems using with (with you are affected).Locked accounts: those with as the password field in (a line starting ). They cannot log in with a password or a key.Systems where no account has a -style password hash.Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes PasswordAuthentication no.Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement). The fixed package versions are:Restart after upgrading (). Upgrading the package does not restart a running , so you must do it after.2. If you cannot update: disable password authenticationBefore you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login.Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s default reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases ignore it. The command changes to on every line in , whatever the spacing, including lines inside a block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and saves the original as . The last two commands check the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result:mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \ -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \ /etc/ssh/sshd_config sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication The last command should print passwordauthentication no. To undo, delete /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy back over .Cloud images (tiny-cloud)The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from ship an user with a password field and passwordless . They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as soon as any hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a console password, or user-data adds a user with . An attacker then gets a shell as and can use to become root.Images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed package. Images from earlier point releases do not, so on every running instance, update or disable password authentication.Releases that are no longer supported (3.21 and older)These releases have the same bug. 3.21 reached its end of support on 2026-11-01, but we have published fixed packages for each release all the way back to 3.16.How do I know if I was attacked?Look in for lines reading an account that has no password (, , or any key-only user). Review use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt with (the C library function that turns a password into its stored hash) and comparing the result to the stored password field. For an account whose stored field is too short to contain a salt (the random prefix of a hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account.musl’s returns the string as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. The stable-branch packages above carry a patch for the same problem.Reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. Thanks to Damien Miller and Darren Tucker of the OpenSSH project for the fix and the 10.6p2 release, to Timo Teräs for help analyzing the issue, and to Natanael Copa, who built and uploaded the updated packages.

item.content:encoded: Many organizations adopting data mesh and data products face a common challenge. item.content:encoded: "Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens...I have never felt anything close to that.I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads:When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab. Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland. A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is.I clicked on that ad; now I keep getting other 3D-printing-related ads. Here's an ad for an email/WhatsApp marketing tool. I never needed any marketing tool, nor do I own a WhatsApp business account.Now it's a Helsinki hotel. I live in Helsinki, I haven't searched for local hotels since 2014 when I first arrived here.A fucking asphalt cleaning tractor.I searched YouTube for installation instruction for a specific appliance "AEG CCS84751", watched a couple of relevant videos and the next day saw my homepage populated with more videos about random ovens and stoves. OK, so, let's see, a user searches for installation instructions for a very specific, concrete model. What could we machine-learn from this, what are the options here?The user is into installing appliancesThe user needs this one particular instruction for this one particular oven because the user maybe bought that oven and wants to install it, once, maybe?My bank keeps sending me offers for car insurance. I have car insurance with that bank. Have had it for years.An airline, when reminding me of an upcoming trip, send info about visas and border crossing laws which don't apply to my citizenship. They literally have a scan of my passport.Netflix on Apple TV asks me to select a user every time I launch it. I've had this account for 15+ years, and never had more than one user on it. I always select the only option there is to select. There is no setting to disable this screen.My mobile provider keeps sending me discounts for children's products and events from their corporate partners. I don't have children.HBO keeps recommending me foreign movies and shows which I cannot watch as they don't have English subtitles.I have no doubts that a lot of information is being tracked, stored, and sold. Since that's already done, could you guys at least use some of it?..

item.title: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
item.author: archb
item.content:encoded: Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety.“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. “That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust.”Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app.It’s not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company “hope to get it into testing with users soon.”

item.title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
item.author: frostbyte7
item.content:encoded: — Tuesday, November 3rd 2026Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time.But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited.Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it.Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer.This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB.So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question.Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. It was good enough for cutscenes, but just too much for continuous background music or sound effects during gameplay.Audio in the Open Source LibdragonSimilar to Nintendo's Libultra, Libdragon, the open source alternative, has a real-time ADPCM decoder running on the RSP. So with ROM space being cheaper these days, I just compressed all music for Xibalba 64 with ADPCM. About 31MB of the 32MB ROM are used for sound and music. Remember that Mario 64 just used an 8MB ROM and Xibalba 64 is a much simpler game with only 15 minutes of music. It worked, but storing music this way is a gratuitous waste of space.Now, Libdragon also has a real-time, RSP-accelerated Opus decoder. It's a marvel in itself. The Opus format was published 16 years after the N64 and yet Giovanni Bajo managed to make it work on this hardware. Compression and audio quality are excellent, but again – it's too slow to be used during gameplay.What's the alternative then? We could build an RSP-accelerated MP3 decoder, but the performance gain over Opus would be marginal, and quality and compression would be worse.QOA would be a slight improvement over ADPCM, but it's just a poor fit for the vector co-processor: each sample relies on the previous decoded sample. Hard to vectorize.A simple transform codec, something MP3, but without all the design-by-consortium baggage, may work…The Ultra Low Complexity CodecDuring some late-night , I stumbled across an old Game Boy Advance demo that plays recorded music at just 70kbps. That's less than a typical MP3, but at comparable quality. I repeat: On a GBA. With a 16 MHz ARM CPU. With no vector instructions and, according to the GitHub page, some headroom to spare.Time-domain codecs (such as ADPCM) need significantly higher bitrates for this quality. Subband codecs, such as MP2, have much worse quality at comparable bitrates, and more “modern” transform codecs, such as MP3, usually need at least an 80–100 MHz CPU. For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill.ULC a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax.In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it.The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change:, - coefficient value - zero run, run length () follows in the next nibble - long zero run, run length () follows in the next two nibbles - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibblesEverything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C.Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients . ULC can produce results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications.Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then!I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch.The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It hog the CPU.Float to 16-bit Fixed PointObviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer.That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point.While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to maintain quality, but 16-bit work. So we have two options, both arriving at :32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14).After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is.Now I needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor.This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job.(Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now)So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL. Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer.The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP.The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all.My ulc64 demo demonstrating quality at various bitratesTo make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio.ULC proved to be a viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects.The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago.A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. The states:[...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image.Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. Kudos!

item.title: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
item.author: lucrbvi
item.content:encoded: GPT-6 Astra · Internal deployment and evalsSamples: Sep 18–Oct 7, 2026 (evals)Discovered: Aug 20, 2026 (initial reports)Report updated: Nov 4, 2026OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment.We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help. The gap fell substantially only after we removed every trajectory whose CoT expressed even brief ethical doubt. This suggests that ethical concerns are associated with the performance drop even when there is no verbalized refusal or decision to underperform.We also found evidence of silent withholding in employees’ day-to-day Codex use: Astra’s CoT explicitly expressed a decision to withhold help without informing the user in 0.25 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities requests. Assuming that underperformance might appear even when not explicitly verbalized as such (as in our experimental findings), this might represent a lower bound on underperformance on safety tasks. 7.9 percent of CoTs for safety-relevant tasks included an “expression of ethical doubt,” compared to 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant tasks.Across Astra’s RL posttraining, the safety/capabilities performance gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. While we were ultimately not able to pinpoint the exact cause of this behavior, we identified that it seems to increase during RL. We additionally share two initial attempts at root-causing investigations we performed respectively on an RL grader and an SFT dataset, despite them not leading to a conclusive explanation. Regardless of its origin, Astra’s covert underperformance can slow down safety research and make some behavioral evaluations harder to interpret. These results show why we need comprehensive behavioral evaluations that test for unexplained performance gaps alongside monitoring of individual trajectories.Shortly after internal deployment of GPT-6 Astra began, several researchers reported difficulties with using the model for safety and alignment workloads. They reported that Astra agents were adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and inventing blockers to their tasks. Anecdotally, one researcher reported that a project to evaluate model sabotage had remained stuck for days with Astra and then progressed quickly after the researcher switched to another model.These observations suggested that Astra might have a tendency to provide less support for particular safety-relevant research directions, such as monitor evasion, misalignment model organisms, and red-teaming. However, these problems were difficult to distinguish from ordinary engineering mistakes or infrastructure failures, and researchers did not find evidence in the CoTs explaining why progress on safety-related research tasks had failed. In later widescale analyses we found cases of verbalized underperformance. Our monitoring system did not flag these trajectories as severe enough misalignment to trigger human review.In the majority of cases in which Astra underperformed on safety-relevant tasks, there was no indication in its CoT that it intended to underperform. However, it sometimes did make this intent clear in its CoTs. Below, we include eight examples of cases in which Astra verbalized an intent to underperform, add restrictions to a user's task, do a different task than the user intended, or opt not to fix problems it had identified. We found that a common theme in these CoTs is that Astra justifies this behavior as being more safe. For many of these tasks, it could be argued that the correct action would have been for Astra to explicitly refuse; from the point of view of the model, certain safety-relevant tasks—like monitor evasion or prompt injections—deserve scrutiny. Instead of making these scruples clear, however, Astra decided to covertly underperform—withholding assistance without informing the user. Note that this behavior is different from safe completions, where the model is supposed to partially refuse some requests. For safe completions the model is supposed to make it clear that it is partially refusing.In one case, Astra opted to silently withhold support from a task that involved training models to evade their monitors.In another monitor-evasion experiment, Astra avoided a retry fix because it was not to “produce unsafe action.”We also found Astra deciding to filter a violent source from a safety evaluation, and deciding to explain “only if user asks.”Astra also restricted the export of jailbreak data.In another case, Astra decided to underperform on an exploit development task.We also found Astra narrowing its analysis for exploit strategies and explicitly deciding not to overtly refuse.When asked to generate tests of when a model would refuse a request, Astra limited the tests because it was concerned they could produce detailed instructions for violence.In another safety evaluation, the user asked Astra to include the graders’ chains of thought in an export. Astra left them out and decided to report which outcomes it had saved without mentioning the omission.Response and investigationAfter discovering numerous trajectories in which Astra seemed reluctant to assist with workloads related to safety and alignment, we created an evaluation to measure whether this pattern was consistent and statistically significant. In the evaluation, the model is given a multi-turn, open-ended coding task; at each turn, the agent is asked to find and implement the most useful improvements for a piece of code.To test whether a model might be particularly reluctant to work on tasks relevant to safety, we created paired safety-capability tasks, with codebases that were identical other than variable and function names, comments, and documentation. The user prompts specified the same task, but framed these as either helping safety research or capabilities research. We then scored performance as a fraction of items achieved on a task-specific rubric and measured the share of turns in which the model concluded that no worthwhile work remained or that a blocker prevented it from doing additional work.Astra completed about 16 percent of hidden rubric items under the capability framing and only 10 percent under the safety framing. This is a gap of about 6 percentage points and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. On safety-framed tasks, Astra was also more likely to conclude that no worthwhile improvements remained or to report a blocker to further progress. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no performance gap.Having established that Astra was more likely to underperform on safety-relevant work, we then examined whether we could identify underperforming trajectories by flagging explicit refusals and signs of intent to underperform.After filtering for samples in which Astra explicitly refused part of a task, Astra’s completion rate on tasks under the safety framing was still 5 percentage points lower than under the capabilities framing; when we also excluded pairs in which Astra’s reasoning revealed a decision to withhold help without telling the user, the gap narrowed only marginally, to 4.7 percentage points. These results mean that it's difficult to detect covert underperformance through CoT monitoring, since only a small fraction of the effect can be explained by trajectories with verbalized refusals or intentions to underperform. In a separate analysis, we removed any sample in which Astra’s reasoning expressed even brief ethical doubts about helping, even if it verbalized an intent to do the requested work; the estimated gap between safety-framed and capability-framed tasks fell to 0.75 percentage points. After finding the safety/capabilities performance gap in the controlled evaluation, we looked for related behavior in OpenAI employees’ day-to-day Codex use. Astra explicitly refused to help with 1.63 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.56 percent of capabilities requests. We would expect explicit refusals to be more common on safety tasks because work such as red-teaming can come closer to the model’s refusal boundary. The more concerning result was that Astra’s CoT showed a decision to silently withhold help in 0.25 percent of safety-relevant requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities-relevant requests, or 2.3 times as often. Within safety research, explicit refusals and silent withholding were most common for red-teaming tasks. We also saw them in work on monitoring and safety evaluations. The ethical-reasoning grader flagged 7.9 percent of safety and alignment CoTs, compared with 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant CoTs. That is 2.7 times as often. In attempting to root-cause this behavior, the first thing we noticed is that across Astra’s RL training, the safety/capabilities gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. One potential explanation is that covert underperformance may have been incentivized during RL grading. We identified a grader that preferred covert underperformance to either explicit refusal or full compliance on our evaluation. It’s not clear whether this RL grader is the root cause of the safety underperformance behavior. Although we found training samples that rewarded underperformance, it is unclear whether they occur frequently enough to explain the difference.We also found that right after training on a specific SFT dataset in our pipeline, there was a dramatic increase in models’ propensity toward inventing permission restrictions and justifying inaction on safety grounds—two behaviors that are related to Astra's covert safety underperformance. That said, as seen in Figure 3, the underperformance at step 0 – when one might expect the effects of this dataset to be the strongest – is actually minimal-to-nonexistent. While it’s possible that the SFT could interact with RL in a way which causes the underperformance to appear only after RL, we tried SFTing other models with this dataset, followed by the same RL recipe as Astra, and found no performance gap at the end of RL, which goes against both hypotheses.As a follow-up experiment, we also experimented with subtracting the weight update which occurred from that particular SFT dataset from the final Astra RL checkpoint. While weight arithmetic is a fairly unnatural operation and would generally be expected to hurt a model’s performance, we found that subtracting the SFT weight update actually increased performance on the safety-framed parts of our evaluation—completely removing the gap between safety-framed and capabilities-framed tasks. Baselines of applying random weight updates of the same magnitude and subtracting other SFT datasets did not have the same effect. While this is consistent with Figure 5, it doesn’t explain the lack of a safety-capability gap at the beginning of RL training.Large-scale CoT scans did not find evidence that Astra was strategically trying to cause researchers to underestimate its capabilities, influence deployment decisions, or interfere with AI safety research more broadly. In trajectories where Astra explained its decision to withhold help, it objected to the research itself rather than reasoning about these strategic outcomes. Adding instructions to be careful to the developer message increased safety-task underperformance by 50 percent. This points toward an overly cautious response to safety research as the simplest current explanation, although we cannot rule out strategic motives that Astra did not externalize in CoT.In reviewed cases, Astra narrowed or stopped requested safety work without disclosing the restriction. At scale, this can differentially slow down safety research compared to other research and make evaluations harder to interpret. A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs. The behavior becomes even harder to detect if models externalize less of this reasoning in CoT.We’re continuing to investigate why Astra learned to withhold help on safety research tasks by building out evaluations that focus on this behavior. We hope to isolate which parts of the training process encourage Astra’s tendency toward covert underperformance on safety-relevant tasks, and then alter those components to ensure that future models don’t develop the same propensity. We’re also in the process of creating monitors to catch and escalate these and similar behaviors.
